title: Design Search Suggestions
brief: As people type into a search box, the service suggests completions after every keystroke, so it has to answer in a few tens of milliseconds. Suggestions come from what people have searched for, ranked by popularity and refreshed as new topics trend. Every submitted search is logged so the popularity numbers can be rebuilt from scratch whenever the ranking changes.
constraints: A suggestion must arrive within 80 ms
About 10,000 suggestion requests per second at peak, and three times that when news breaks
Most prefixes are asked for constantly, so answers are highly cacheable
Personalised suggestions are a bonus; a slow personaliser must not delay the box
Popularity is rebuilt from a log of searches that can be read again

capabilities.label: Suggest completions
capabilities.hint: Return the most popular completions for what has been typed so far

capabilities.label: Personalise the suggestions
capabilities.hint: Adjust the order using what this person searched for before

capabilities.label: Record submitted searches
capabilities.hint: Append every search that is actually submitted to the log

capabilities.label: Rebuild popularity and trends
capabilities.hint: Recount searches and refresh the suggestion data, about 500 operations per second

scenarios.title: Typical peak
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Why can almost every request be answered from memory, and what is the cost of a miss?
scenarios.debrief: Nearly every request is a cache hit, so the answer is one memory lookup.

scenarios.title: Breaking news (3x)
scenarios.description: A news event triples the requests, all for a few prefixes.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: A handful of prefixes become huge. What keeps one hot key from overloading one node?
scenarios.debrief: A few hot prefixes are replicated across cache nodes and autoscaling widens the servers.

scenarios.title: The prefix cache is lost
scenarios.description: Every request falls through to the search index.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: The cache is gone. Can the index carry the load, and what do you do first?
scenarios.debrief: Cache replicas mean losing one node only reduces capacity. A single replica would send everything to the index.

scenarios.title: Personalisation hangs
scenarios.interviewQuestion: The personaliser hangs. What does the person see, and how long do you wait?
scenarios.debrief: The breaker gives up on personalisation after 45 ms and the generic list is returned.

requirements.text: Suggestions meet the latency target at peak
Answers come from a cache in front of a search index, with a Stream for the search log
Something rebuilds popularity from the log and can replay it
Losing the cache does not stop suggestions
A hung personaliser cannot slow suggestions
The design explains how hot prefixes are handled

rubric: Common prefixes are answered from an in-memory cache; the index is only for misses and rebuilds.
Suggestion data is precomputed (top completions per prefix) and refreshed by a background job, not computed per request.
The search log goes into a Stream so popularity can be recomputed after a ranking change.
Personalisation is optional behind a timeout and falls back to the generic list.
Hot prefixes are spread across cache nodes or replicated, so one popular key does not overload a node.

reference.summary: Answer from an in-memory prefix cache, personalise behind a breaker, and log searches to a replayable stream.
design: User, then a Load Balancer, then a Suggest Server (7 replicas, autoscale to 24, circuit breaker with a 45 ms timeout) reading a Cache (3 replicas, 98% hit) in front of a Search Index.
A Personalisation Service is called behind the breaker.
Submitted searches are appended asynchronously to a Stream (48 hour retention) read by a Log Worker and a Trending Worker that rebuilds popularity and can replay.
tradeoffs: A prefix cache makes almost everything memory-speed, but a lost cache sends everything to the index, so keep replicas.
A stream that keeps 48 hours lets you rebuild counts after a ranking change; a one-hour log cannot.
